subject: CIVICS
name: The Indian Constitution
summary: The rules that bind the government, and why they were written down.
source: NCERT Class 8 Political Science (Social and Political Life III), syllabus topic coverage only

questions.stem: On which date did the Constitution of India come into effect?
choices: 26 January 1950
15 August 1947
26 November 1949
2 October 1950
questions.solution: The Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 but came into force on 26 January 1950, which is why that day is Republic Day. The date was chosen deliberately: 26 January 1930 had been observed as Purna Swaraj day, so the Republic began on the anniversary of the demand for complete independence. 15 August 1947 is Independence Day, a different thing — a country can be independent without yet being a republic.

questions.stem: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution?
choices: Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Dr Rajendra Prasad
Jawaharlal Nehru
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
questions.solution: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee and is the figure most closely associated with the text of the Constitution. Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly as a whole and later became the first President; Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution and became the first Prime Minister; Patel chaired several committees and led the integration of the princely states. All four were central, which is why they are offered together.

questions.stem: What does federalism mean in the Indian context?
choices: The existence of more than one level of government, each with its own powers
That all power rests with the central government in New Delhi
That each state may make its own constitution and leave the union
That the government must be elected every five years
questions.solution: Federalism means there is more than one tier of government — the Union, the states, and since 1992 the local bodies — each with powers assigned to it by the Constitution rather than granted at the pleasure of the tier above. The Constitution divides subjects into Union, State and Concurrent lists to make this concrete. Indian federalism is deliberately strong at the centre, but a state's powers are still constitutional, not a favour.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that India is a secular state?
choices: The state does not have an official religion and does not favour or discriminate on religious grounds
Citizens are discouraged from practising any religion
Only the majority religion may be practised publicly
Religious institutions run the government
questions.solution: Indian secularism means the state adopts no official religion, gives none preferential treatment, and protects every citizen's freedom to practise, profess and propagate their own — or none. It is not hostility to religion, which is the usual misreading. It is also not identical to the strict separation model used in some other countries: the Indian state may intervene in religious practice to protect fundamental rights, as it did in abolishing untouchability.

questions.stem: Under which Fundamental Right does the abolition of untouchability fall?
choices: The Right to Equality
The Right to Freedom
The Right against Exploitation
The Right to Freedom of Religion
questions.solution: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form, and it sits within the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18). The placement is the point: untouchability was treated as a denial of equal status, not merely as ill-treatment. The Right against Exploitation is a genuine right and a plausible distractor, but it deals with forced labour, trafficking and child labour in hazardous work.

questions.stem: What does the separation of powers achieve?
choices: It divides power among the legislature, executive and judiciary so that each can check the others
It separates the central government from the state governments
It divides the country into states and union territories
It separates religion from politics
questions.solution: The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary interprets them and rules on disputes. Keeping the three in different hands means no single organ can both make a rule and be the final judge of it. The division into central and state governments is a real and important division too, but that is federalism — a vertical split, where separation of powers is a horizontal one.

questions.stem: Why does a country need its constitution to be a written document rather than a set of understood conventions?
choices: Because a written text can be pointed to and enforced in court when those in power act against it
Because written documents are easier to change than conventions
Because international law requires every country to have one
Because a written constitution guarantees that no government will ever misuse power
questions.solution: A constitution exists chiefly to limit those who hold power, and a limit that lives only in custom can be denied by whoever is strong enough to deny it. Writing it down makes the limits citable — a citizen can go to court and point at a clause. The last option is worth rejecting explicitly: writing rules down does not prevent abuse, it makes abuse identifiable and challengeable, which is a more modest and more honest claim.

questions.stem: Why did Dr Ambedkar call the Right to Constitutional Remedies the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
choices: Because it lets a citizen approach the courts directly when any other Fundamental Right is violated, which is what makes the other rights real
Because it is the longest of the Fundamental Rights
Because it grants the government power to suspend rights in an emergency
Because it establishes the Supreme Court
questions.solution: A right with no way to enforce it is a statement of intent. Article 32 allows a citizen whose Fundamental Right has been violated to move the Supreme Court directly, and the court can issue writs to compel or forbid action. That enforcement mechanism is what converts the other rights from promises into claims, which is precisely why Ambedkar singled it out.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy?
choices: Fundamental Rights are enforceable in court; Directive Principles are guidelines the state should follow but cannot be sued over
Fundamental Rights apply to citizens and Directive Principles apply to foreigners
Directive Principles are enforceable and Fundamental Rights are only advisory
Fundamental Rights can be amended and Directive Principles cannot
questions.solution: Fundamental Rights are justiciable: a citizen can go to court to enforce them. Directive Principles set out goals for governance — adequate livelihood, free and compulsory education for children, equal pay — that the state is directed to work towards, but a citizen cannot sue the government for failing to achieve them. The distinction reflects a practical judgement of the Constituent Assembly: some things a poor new state could guarantee immediately, and others it could only commit to pursuing.

questions.stem: In India's parliamentary system, to whom is the executive answerable on a day-to-day basis?
choices: To the legislature, which can remove the government by withdrawing its confidence
To the President alone, who appoints and dismisses ministers at will
To the Supreme Court, which reviews every decision it takes
To no one between elections
questions.solution: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are drawn from the legislature and remain in office only while they command the confidence of the Lok Sabha, which can remove them by a vote of no confidence. That is the defining feature of a parliamentary system as against a presidential one, where the executive is separately elected for a fixed term. It means accountability is continuous rather than only at election time.

questions.stem: Fundamental Rights are not absolute — reasonable restrictions may be placed on them. Who decides whether a particular restriction is reasonable?
choices: The courts, which review the restriction against the Constitution
The Prime Minister, as head of the government
Parliament alone, whose decision on this is final
Nobody; any restriction passed as law is automatically valid
questions.solution: The Constitution itself allows restrictions on rights such as free speech — for public order, decency, the security of the state and so on — so the existence of a limit is not by itself unconstitutional. What keeps this from swallowing the right is that the judiciary decides whether a given restriction is reasonable, striking down those that are not. If Parliament were the final judge of the limits on rights that constrain Parliament, the constraint would be meaningless, which is the reasoning the question is aimed at.

questions.stem: The 'basic structure' doctrine holds that Parliament may amend the Constitution but not alter its essential features. What problem does this solve?
choices: That an unlimited amending power would let a temporary majority dismantle the very rights and structures the Constitution exists to protect
That the Constitution was too short and needed to be lengthened
That state governments were amending the Constitution without permission
That the Constitution contained no provision for amendment at all
questions.solution: The Constitution has to be amendable, or it could not adapt; but if the amending power were unlimited, a government with the required majority could amend away judicial review, federalism or the Fundamental Rights themselves — using the Constitution's own procedure to end what it protects. The doctrine, established in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), holds that amendments cannot destroy the basic structure. The genuine tension is worth naming: it places an unelected judiciary above an elected Parliament on this one question, and defenders and critics both start from that fact.
